lead: A surface in space can be written as F(x, y, z) = 0. At any point P on it, the gradient ∇F gives one vector that points straight out of the surface. That single vector builds two objects: the plane that just touches the surface at P, and the line that pierces it there. The plane is what the surface looks like under a microscope, so it is used to read slopes of hills, set cutting tools in a workshop, and compute lighting in 3D graphics.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for partial derivatives and Chapter 4.3 for the total differential as the change along a tangent plane.

sections.h3: The gradient is perpendicular to the surface

blocks.text: The level curve f(x, y) = c has a gradient ∇f = (f_x, f_y) that is perpendicular to it, and Chapter 4.7 used exactly that. The same idea lifts to three variables.

Write the surface as F(x, y, z) = c, where F is a function of three variables and c is a constant. Move everything to one side so that c = 0. Take any smooth curve r(t) = (x(t), y(t), z(t)) lying on the surface and passing through P at t = 0.

Along that curve F(r(t)) = c for every t. Differentiate with the chain rule: F_x x′(t) + F_y y′(t) + F_z z′(t) = 0, that is ∇F · r′(t) = 0. The vector r′(0) is a tangent direction of the surface at P. Every tangent direction at P comes from some such curve, so ∇F is perpendicular to all of them at once.

So ∇F at P is the normal vector to the surface at P. One condition is needed: ∇F ≠ 0 at P. Where the gradient vanishes the point is singular and may have no single tangent plane, like the tip of a cone.

blocks.where: F_x = ∂F/∂x at P, and similarly F_y, F_z; n is perpendicular to the surface F = 0 at P.

blocks.text: The tangent plane at P = (x₀, y₀, z₀) is the plane through P perpendicular to n. A point (x, y, z) lies on it exactly when the vector (x − x₀, y − y₀, z − z₀), which joins P to that point, is perpendicular to n.
F_x(x − x₀) + F_y(y − y₀) + F_z(z − z₀) = 0
blocks.where: the three partials are numbers, evaluated at P; (x₀, y₀, z₀) is the point of contact.

blocks.text: The normal line is the line through P along n, so its direction ratios are the same three partials.

blocks.where: each denominator is that partial derivative evaluated at P; these are direction ratios, not lengths.

blocks.text: If a partial is zero, do not divide by it. Keep that equation in product form: F_y = 0 means y = y₀, and the other two ratios are equal.

items: Move everything to one side to get F(x, y, z) = 0.
Differentiate to get F_x, F_y, F_z.
Substitute P = (x₀, y₀, z₀) into all three.
Put P and n into F_x(x − x₀) + F_y(y − y₀) + F_z(z − z₀) = 0.
Simplify, then check that P satisfies the plane equation.

sections.h3: Surfaces given as z = f(x, y)

blocks.text: Most surfaces here arrive as z = f(x, y). Put F = f(x, y) − z. Then F_x = f_x, F_y = f_y and F_z = −1, so at P the normal is (f_x, f_y, −1).
The minus sign on the z-component is not decoration. Using (f_x, f_y, +1) gives f_x Δx + f_y Δy + (z − z₀) = 0, which rearranges to z − z₀ = −f_x Δx − f_y Δy: every slope comes out reversed.

Solved for z, the correct plane reads z = z₀ + f_x Δx + f_y Δy, where Δx = x − x₀ and Δy = y − y₀. That is the total differential of Chapter 4.3, Δz ≈ f_x Δx + f_y Δy. The tangent plane is the linear approximation, drawn.
Two surfaces meeting at P meet at the angle between their normals n₁ and n₂: cos θ = (n₁ · n₂)/(|n₁||n₂|), where the dot is the sum of products and |n| is the length √(n₁² + n₂² + n₃²).

The tangent plane also tracks the surface near P: any small step along the plane changes z by the total differential, so it is the flat stand-in for the surface in error estimates and in optimisation.

figure.caption: At P = (1, 2, 5) on the bowl z = x² + y² the gradient (2, 4, −1) is the normal. The plane through P perpendicular to it is 2x + 4y − z = 5, and the line along it is the normal line.

spec.aria: A downward flow from the surface with point P to its gradient, then branching to the tangent plane equation and the normal line ratios.

examples.question: Find the tangent plane and the normal line to the surface z = x² + y² at the point P = (1, 2, 5).
steps: Check that P lies on the surface: x² + y² = 1² + 2² = 1 + 4 = 5, and z = 5. Yes.
Write the surface in implicit form: F(x, y, z) = x² + y² − z, so F = 0 on the surface.
Expand: 2x − 2 + 4y − 8 − z + 5 = 0, so 2x + 4y − z − 5 = 0, that is 2x + 4y − z = 5.
Check with P: 2(1) + 4(2) − 5 = 2 + 8 − 5 = 5. The plane passes through P.
Read as a linear approximation: z = 5 + 2(x − 1) + 4(y − 2), matching Δz ≈ f_x Δx + f_y Δy with f_x = 2 and f_y = 4.
examples.answer: The tangent plane is 2x + 4y − z = 5 and the normal line is (x − 1)/2 = (y − 2)/4 = (z − 5)/(−1).
examples.check:
x0, y0, z0 = 1, 2, 5

Fy = 2*y0
Fz = -1
print(Fx)
print(Fy)
print(Fz)
print(Fx*x0 + Fy*y0 + Fz*z0)

traps: For z = f(x, y) the normal is (f_x, f_y, −1), not (f_x, f_y, +1). With +1 the plane equation reverses the sign of both slopes.
Evaluate the partials at P before writing the plane. A plane equation still containing x and y is not a plane.
The gradient of F has three components; the gradient of f has two. Do not drop the z-entry.
If a partial vanishes at P, do not put a zero in a denominator. Write that variable as equal to its value at P and equate the other two ratios.
Check the final plane by substituting P. A sign slip in the constant is the most common lost mark in this question.

quiz.q: State the normal vector to a surface F(x, y, z) = 0 at a point P on it.
quiz.a: n = (F_x, F_y, F_z), all three partials evaluated at P, and this needs ∇F ≠ 0 at P.

quiz.q: Why is ∇F perpendicular to the surface F(x, y, z) = 0?
quiz.a: Take any curve r(t) on the surface through P. F(r(t)) is constant, so the chain rule gives ∇F · r′(t) = 0. Thus ∇F is perpendicular to every tangent direction at P.

quiz.q: Find the tangent plane to the sphere x² + y² + z² = 14 at (1, 2, 3).
Find the tangent plane and normal line to z = xy at (2, 3, 6).
Find the angle between the surfaces x² + y² + z² = 6 and z = x² + y² at the point (1, 1, 2).
A student writes the tangent plane to z = x² + y² at (1, 2, 5) as 2(x − 1) + 4(y − 2) + (z − 5) = 0. What is wrong, and what plane did the student actually get?
quiz.a: The z-component of the normal must be −1, because F = x² + y² − z. The student used (2, 4, 1). The plane 2x + 4y + z = 15 does pass through P, but its slopes are reversed, so it is not tangent to the bowl.

quiz.q: What does the tangent plane tell you numerically about f near P?
quiz.a: It is the linear approximation: z = z₀ + f_x Δx + f_y Δy. For small steps, the change in z is the total differential, and the error shrinks faster than the step size.

beyond: Not for the exam. Every 3D rendering engine stores a normal per vertex and uses it to shade the surface; the tangent plane then fixes the local frame for texture mapping. Computer-aided machining converts a designed surface into cutter paths from the same normals, and terrain software reports slope and aspect of a hillside as the tilt of the tangent plane. In machine learning, the gradient is the normal to a level set of the loss, which is why gradient descent steps across level sets. Search next for surface normals in computer graphics, tool-path generation in CAD, and the tangent plane in gradient descent.
